# Module 4. A worked example, end to end {#sec-m4}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**In this chapter.** Run one country the whole way through, from parameter choices to publishable prose. Uganda is the worked case: the tool's golden-master verification country, every figure checkable against two published documents. The scaffolding then fades, through a completion problem on Ethiopia where you finish the interpretation, to an independent problem on a third country done alone. The target is a write-up rather than a chart, in the format of the IMF's C-PIMA presentation of Q-CRAFT results and Section III of Uganda's Fiscal Risk Statement.

There is no short route through this chapter, because it is the one the capstone is built from. If time is short, do [the Uganda run](#sec-m4-worked), all seven steps, and [the unscaffolded third-country problem](#sec-m4-independent), and skip the middle.
:::

## Two documents already show what the output looks like

You are not inventing a format. Two published documents show how Q-CRAFT output reads when it reaches a policymaker. Both are about Uganda, where the tool has run the full cycle from workshop to published statement. The genre is not Ugandan, and your ministry's version will look much the same.

The IMF's C-PIMA write-up covers the whole assessment in a single paragraph. *Uganda: PFM Climate Assessment: Public Investment and Fiscal Risks Management* [(IMF, 2024)](references.qmd#src-imf-2024-uganda) reports the September 2023 workshop with staff of Uganda's Ministry of Finance, Planning and Economic Development (MoFPED, the finance ministry). Climate change looks milder in Uganda than in other sub-Saharan African countries, it says, yet still matters for growth and fiscal sustainability: by end of century GDP loss could pass 4 percentage points, with debt at 66 percent of GDP against 47.5 percent in the baseline. That one paragraph carries three numbers and a comparative judgment.

Uganda's Fiscal Risk Statement FY 2024/25, published by MoFPED, is the fuller treatment. It carries scenario definitions, a baseline fiscal path table, GDP deviation charts, fiscal balance and debt charts, and a closing policy sentence. Its climate section runs pages 13 to 17 of a 31-page document, and three source lines under its exhibits read "QCRAFT (2023)."

**Your capstone is the shorter of the two.** This module builds it.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The published section, page by page

Every line below is from the document itself: open it and check.

Page 4, the introduction. The statement groups fiscal risks into three categories and says the climate analysis "expanded its scope on fiscal risks associated with climate change by using the Quantitative Climate Risk Assessment Fiscal Tool (Q-CRAFT) for long term fiscal sustainability analysis." That is the tool named in the ministry's own words, in the framing section.

Page 13, the section opens. The body heading reads "III. CLIMATE CHANGE AND NATURAL DISASTER FISCAL RISKS". The table of contents lists the same section as "CLIMATE CHANGE FISCAL RISKS". The page is national hazard context rather than Q-CRAFT output: floods and epidemics at about 75 percent of recorded events between 1985 and 2021, footnoted to the World Bank's Climate Risk Country Profile 2021, and annual economic losses from natural disasters estimated at US$87 million. Table 4 is sourced to the World Bank Group (2022).

Pages 14 to 15, the set-up. "Using the Q-craft tool, an assessment of the impact of climate change on Uganda's economic growth and fiscal sustainability was undertaken." The tool quantifies effects "under five different climate scenarios, against a baseline", the five named and defined on the page: Paris, Moderate, High, Hot, Vulnerable. A footnote cites [Kahn et al. (2021)](references.qmd#src-kahn-2021) for the temperature-to-growth empirics. Page 15 carries Figure 8, the baseline decomposition of nominal GDP growth, and Table 5, the baseline fiscal path reproduced below, under the line "Source (Fig 8 & Tab 5: QCRAFT (2023)".

Page 16, the macroeconomic effects. Figure 9, deviations from the baseline in level GDP and in labour productivity growth, "Source: QCRAFT (2023)". The text reports "a 4 percent reduction in nominal GDP by the end of the century under the Hot scenario", with Paris and Moderate described as benign for Uganda.

Page 17, the fiscal effects and the finding. Figures 10 and 11, balances and the debt ratio by scenario, "Source: QCRAFT (2023)". Then the two sentences the whole section exists for: the primary deficit under Hot ends "0.7 percent worse than the baseline, thereby raising public debt by over 18 percent of GDP", and "In the High, Hot, and Vulnerable scenarios, public debt surpasses the 50 percent of GDP fiscal rule ceiling, taking on an unsustainable upward trajectory." The section closes on a policy sentence about meeting Paris commitments.

The section runs five pages and carries one table, four figures, and one threshold finding. Your two paragraphs are the Q-CRAFT core of a section that size.
:::

{{< include figures/_course-map-m4.qmd >}}

## The target format {#sec-m4-target}

**The Q-CRAFT part of the Statement's climate section is organised in three moves, numbered in the document itself.** Copy that structure. It is the one MoFPED published, in the document its own readers use.

| Move | What it contains | Where your material comes from |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Set up the analysis** | What the tool does, the scenarios used, and the baseline fiscal path | [Module 3](m3-parameters.qmd) parameters, Baseline tab |
| **2. Macroeconomic effects** | GDP deviation from baseline by scenario, and the productivity channel behind it | Climate tab for the deviation chart; Step 3 of [Module 2](m2-debt-equation.qmd) for the productivity mechanism |
| **3. Fiscal effects** | Primary and overall balance by scenario, debt-to-GDP by scenario, read against the fiscal anchor | Analysis tab for the debt chart; the exported results (the packet's CSV or its Excel file, Step 6) for the balance series |

The published baseline table is worth copying too. Uganda's Table 5 reports four years, not seventy:

| Summary fiscal path | 2023 | 2050 | 2075 | 2099 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Primary expenditure (% of GDP) | 19.9 | 19.6 | 18.8 | 19.4 |
| Interest expenditure (% of GDP) | 3.3 | 1.3 | 1.8 | 2.4 |
| Interest rate (%) | 7.7 | 3.9 | 5.5 | 5.5 |
| Primary balance (% of GDP) | -6.3 | -1.7 | -0.8 | -1.4 |
| Overall balance (% of GDP) | -9.6 | -3.0 | -2.7 | -3.8 |
| Debt-to-GDP ratio (%) | 47.1 | 36.2 | 35.8 | 47.5 |

Source: Uganda Fiscal Risk Statement FY 2024/25, Table 5, sourced to QCRAFT (2023).

Four columns is a deliberate editorial choice, because a seventy-row table is not a policy document. Before any climate damage, the baseline says this: debt falls to the mid-30s by mid-century and comes back to 47.5 by 2099. The interest rate row, read against the growth path, shows why.

## The worked case: Uganda, start to finish {#sec-m4-worked}

**Uganda is the worked case because its numbers are published and checkable, not because it is the country you work on.** What transfers is the method: the seven steps below. Work through them in the app. Every step names what you are doing and what it licenses you to say.

The figure below lays the seven out, with step 3 across the middle rather than beside the others.

{{< include figures/_m4-seven-steps.qmd >}}

Every step after that gate is only as good as the baseline beneath it, so the sanity check comes before any climate reading.

### Step 1: set the parameters, and write down why

Two questions from [Module 3](m3-parameters.qmd) and [Module 1](m1-how-qcraft-thinks.qmd), without looking back:

1. Which two choices change the climate result but not the baseline?
2. In which year do climate scenarios begin to diverge from the baseline?

(Answers: expenditure rigidity, and the climate scenario itself. Everything else moves both. 2030.)

Open [Q-CRAFT Explorer](https://teal-insights.github.io/QCraft-App/explorer/) and select Uganda. Use these settings for the worked case:

| Parameter | Setting | Rationale for the packet |
|---|---|---|
| Country | Uganda | Analysis subject |
| Demography variant | Medium | Reference variant, with Low tested as a sensitivity |
| Debt target | 50% of GDP | The ceiling Uganda's own Fiscal Risk Statement reads results against |
| Fiscal rule | On for the headline run | The setting the published workbook ships, so the headline run is the one a reader can reproduce in Excel, with the rule-off run reported alongside as the sensitivity |
| Expenditure rigidity | 1.0 | Tool default, conservative, with budget composition evidence per [Module 3](m3-parameters.qmd) and 0.6 tested as a sensitivity |

**That table is the first page of your export packet.** Write it before looking at any output, so the settings are choices rather than post-hoc justifications. The five controls under Growth assumptions stay at engine defaults for the worked case. The annex records that they were left there, and the standard in [Module 3](m3-parameters.qmd) asks for one line more: that the global productivity and inflation paths were read against Uganda's own record and kept, because nothing in that record argues for moving them. Write that line into the analyst's note.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Going deeper: why the rule is on, and what happens when it is off

Turning the fiscal rule off looks like the more neutral choice. It is not.

With the rule off, Uganda's baseline debt ratio falls to zero by 2050 and stays there. The climate scenarios keep going, landing between -474 and -523 percent of GDP by 2099. Their order inverts on the way, Paris-Aligned finishing lowest and Hot + Unadapted highest, so the chart appears to say the hottest future is the best fiscal outcome.

Nothing has gone wrong. That is the workbook's own arithmetic. On the `Baseline` sheet the debt recursion is wrapped in a floor, `=IF((...)<0,0,(...))`, so a negative baseline is written as zero. The six scenario sheets carry no floor. [The debt floor rule in Module 5](m5-boundaries.qmd#sec-m5-floor) sets out the asymmetry and the reading rule for charts that touch zero.

A rule-off baseline is not assumption-free. It is a baseline pinned to a floor, compared against scenarios that have none, and the comparison stops meaning anything. The rule-on run is also the setting the published workbook ships, at cell `C33` of its Dashboard, so a reader can reproduce it in Excel step for step.

Report the rule-off run as a sensitivity if you want it, and say in the packet
which years the floor is active. Do not put it in the headline.
:::

### Step 2: read the Baseline tab {#sec-m4-baseline}

**The Baseline tab shows the no-climate-change scenario: the country's fiscal trajectory under current trends and the assumptions you set.** Three charts share the tab.

Debt-to-GDP trajectory (first) is the headline chart. Follow it out of the shaded region (the WEO record and forecast) into the model's own projection. Is debt rising, stable, or falling? With the fiscal rule on, debt should converge toward your target. With it off, the trajectory reveals the underlying fiscal dynamics: favourable when growth exceeds interest rates, unfavourable when interest rates exceed growth.

Revenue and Expenditure (% of GDP) (second) shows two ratios that can drift apart. Revenue-to-GDP stays constant by assumption: revenue grows with nominal GDP. Primary expenditure-to-GDP may diverge: spending follows total population, revenue the working-age population, with productivity and inflation common to both sides. Where working-age population outgrows total (the demographic dividend), expenditure-to-GDP falls and fiscal space opens. In ageing countries it rises, a structural fiscal pressure independent of any policy choice.

Fiscal Balances (third) carries two lines: the primary balance, revenue minus non-interest expenditure, and the overall balance, which includes interest payments. The zero line is the reference: a primary surplus means non-interest revenue covers non-interest spending. The gap between the lines is the interest burden on existing debt.

{{< include figures/_screenshot-m4-baseline.qmd >}}

### Step 3: run the sanity check before you interpret anything {#sec-m4-sanity}

::: {.callout-tip}
## Baseline Sanity Check

Before interpreting climate results, verify the baseline makes sense:

- [ ] Does the initial debt level match your country's actual current debt-to-GDP ratio?
- [ ] Is the revenue-to-GDP ratio plausible given WEO forecasts?
- [ ] Does the expenditure path reflect realistic spending trends?
- [ ] If the fiscal rule is on, does debt converge toward your target?
- [ ] Do the primary and overall balance paths make economic sense given the country's fiscal history?
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## DRAFT FOR TEAL: the sanity check applied to Uganda

Initial debt level: the published 47.1 percent of GDP for 2023 agrees with the ministry's own 46.9 at June 2023. If your Explorer run differs materially, the likely cause is the WEO vintage: Current mode runs WEO April 2026, Verified mode the workbook's own October 2024, and the published table came from the 2023 run. Note the difference rather than fixing it by overriding data.

Revenue-to-GDP: the check is whether the level is right, because the share is held constant by construction. For a country midway through a revenue mobilisation strategy, a flat revenue ratio is a conservative assumption worth one sentence in the write-up.

Expenditure path: the published table has primary expenditure drifting from 19.9 to 19.4 percent of GDP over seventy-six years, dipping to 18.8 around 2075. That is the demographic dividend: total population growth drives spending, working-age growth drives GDP, and for a while the second outruns the first. If your path rises instead of drifting down, check the demography variant.

Fiscal rule convergence: Uganda's debt converges toward the target from below. Note in your packet that convergence from below means the rule is not binding on this path, so the target is not doing the work the trajectory suggests.

Balance paths: the published primary deficit narrows from 6.3 percent of GDP in 2023 to 1.4 by 2099, with the overall deficit at 3.8. That is a large near-term consolidation built into the WEO forecast period, not something the model invented. Whether it is credible is a question about the WEO, and belongs in the write-up as a caveat rather than a correction.

**The rule this step encodes: a climate result computed on a baseline you have not checked is a number with no owner.** Every one of the five boxes is a question someone will ask you.
:::

### Step 4: read the Climate tab

The Climate tab shows how climate change affects real GDP under six warming scenarios, using empirical estimates from the FADCP Climate Dataset [(Centorrino, Massetti, and Tagklis, 2024)](references.qmd#src-centorrino-2024), building on [Kahn et al. (2021)](references.qmd#src-kahn-2021).

The Briefing view, the default, shows one chart: real GDP under each scenario as a percentage deviation from the baseline path, so you read the damage rather than the growth. The Workbook view shows the same content as the workbook draws it: absolute GDP levels and a GDP index set to 100 in 2029. The six scenarios run from Paris-Aligned (below 2°C warming by 2100) to Hot + Unadapted (high warming with slow adaptation). Impacts begin in 2030, and before that every scenario sits on the baseline.

**The size of the modelled loss is country-specific even though the response rate is pooled.** The estimates apply historical relationships between temperature deviations and output to each country's own projected warming path and historical norm (Step 3b of [Module 2](m2-debt-equation.qmd)), so the same scenario hits two economies differently. The C-PIMA summary describes Uganda's impact as milder than other sub-Saharan African countries [(IMF, 2024)](references.qmd#src-imf-2024-uganda).

A country showing a large gap between Paris and Hot + Unadapted faces high climate-fiscal vulnerability. A small gap suggests lower direct climate exposure in the model, though Q-CRAFT's conservative methodology omits indirect effects: natural disasters, sea-level rise, and spillovers such as trade disruptions.

::: {.callout-important}
## DRAFT FOR TEAL: what the Uganda GDP chart licenses you to say

The published result is a level GDP loss of around 4 percent by end of century under the Hot scenario.

Four percent needs a perspective sentence: on its own it reads as small. Two are available, pointing in opposite directions, so pick deliberately and say which you picked.

The deflating one: 4 percent of GDP spread over seventy-five years is a few hundredths of a percentage point off annual growth, well inside the noise of any single year's outturn.

The alarming one: it is a permanent level loss that compounds into the debt ratio every year thereafter, and a recurring annual amount of that size is worth setting against a named line of your own approved budget. Take that budget figure from your own approved estimates rather than from memory, because the ministry you are writing for publishes the actual number.

::: {.callout-warning .authoring-note}
## TODO: verify the perspective figure
Before this ships, source the comparator for the worked case itself: 4 percent of Uganda's GDP against a named line of the approved budget (health, or the road sector), from the Approved Estimates for the relevant year. Do not ship an approximate comparison in a document aimed at the ministry that publishes the actual number.
:::

Both framings are true. The second is what a fiscal risk statement is for. The first is what a sceptical reader will send back. Write the paragraph so it survives both.

**What the chart does not license: any statement about what Uganda's GDP will be.** This is a deviation between two runs of the same model, not a growth forecast.
:::

{{< include figures/_screenshot-m4-climate-index.qmd >}}

### Step 5: read the Analysis tab {#sec-m4-analysis}

The Analysis tab is the comparison view, overlaying baseline and all climate scenario debt trajectories on a single chart. The spread between them is the additional debt burden attributable to climate change. Three factors set that spread.

1. Climate exposure: how much GDP the country loses under each scenario, from the Climate tab.
2. Expenditure rigidity: how much of the GDP loss passes through to the primary balance and debt. Higher rigidity means a wider spread.
3. Starting fiscal position: countries with unfavourable baseline debt dynamics, where interest exceeds growth, see climate shocks amplified through the debt dynamics equation.

**If baseline debt holds stable or falls while the Hot + Unadapted path rises rapidly, climate change could destabilize an otherwise sustainable fiscal position.** That is the core finding Q-CRAFT is designed to surface: even if our fiscal policy is sound today, could climate change make it unsustainable?

The figure below marks the three readings on a real fan chart.

{{< include figures/_m4-fan-readings.qmd >}}

The flat stretch to 2030 is the reminder that none of this is a forecast of the next decade.

::: {.callout-important}
## Two sets of Uganda numbers sit in this chapter, and comparing them takes care
The fan chart above is the Explorer's own run, on WEO October 2024 at the tool's default settings. The prose quotes the published 2023 workshop, an earlier vintage with its own parameter choices. Compare them scenario by scenario, never across scenarios.

- Baseline against baseline, the two nearly agree: 47 on the chart, 47.5 in the published figures.
- Hot against Hot, they are 28 points apart: 94 on the chart, 66 in the published figures. That distance is vintage and parameter choice, which is the point [Module 1](m1-how-qcraft-thinks.qmd) makes in the abstract, arriving here on a chart.
- The chart's highest line, 127, is Hot + Unadapted, the scenario the Statement calls Vulnerable. It is not the partner for the published 66, and this course does not carry a published end-century figure for it.

One further gap to know before you try to reproduce the chart: it runs at the tool's default 60 percent debt target, while Step 1 above sets 50 percent, the ceiling Uganda's own Statement reads against. Your run of Step 1 will not land on these numbers.
:::

::: {.callout-warning .authoring-note}

## DRAFT FOR TEAL: reading the Uganda fan chart

The gap: baseline at 47.5 percent of GDP in 2099, Hot at 66. Eighteen and a half percentage points is the number for the first sentence. Uganda's Statement says the same from the other end: the primary deficit under Hot ends 0.7 percentage points worse than baseline, "thereby raising public debt by over 18 percent of GDP." A 0.7 point annual deficit gap producing an 18 point debt gap is the compounding traced in Step 3 of [Module 2](m2-debt-equation.qmd), worth saying out loud because non-specialists miss it.

**The threshold: the gap becomes a policy fact only when it crosses something.** Uganda's Statement reports that in the High, Hot and Vulnerable scenarios debt passes the 50 percent of GDP fiscal rule ceiling. That sentence does more work than the 18 points: it converts a projection into a breach of an existing commitment.

The shape: look at when the lines separate, as well as where they end. Scenarios are identical until 2030, then fan slowly. A path crossing the ceiling in 2085 and one crossing in 2060 imply very different urgency, a difference the fan chart shows at a glance and a 2099 table does not.

If your run has debt rising in the baseline, the climate gap is no longer the interesting number, because the baseline and the scenario you are comparing it against are both unsustainable. Say so, and report the year each of the two crosses the anchor instead.
:::

### Step 6: export the packet {#sec-m4-export}

The Data tab holds an interactive data grid, a scenario selector, and two CSV downloads.

- Download this scenario (CSV): the scenario selected above the grid, Baseline as the tab opens. Useful for folding the baseline projection into your own fiscal framework or DSA.
- Download all scenarios (CSV): baseline plus all six climate scenarios, stacked with a scenario column. For custom analysis, cross-country comparison, or integration with other tools.

Every column is a share of GDP or a rate, in percent, and both files carry the run manifest below the data: the same settings record that the packet's run file restores. The grid runs from 2009 through 2099: the WEO record and forecast, then the projection.

The Export tab assembles the packet proper. One zip holds a read-me, the scenario report, an Excel file, the chart pack, the results CSV, the standalone charts, and a run file that restores the whole configuration on import. The assumptions annex prints all ten parameters with the rationale lines you wrote in the sidebar, and where you wrote none it says so. Add a run label and an analyst's note before downloading: both travel into every file.

**The packet is the deliverable: inputs, rationale and output in one place, reproducible by someone who has never met you.** Download it, and keep it with the parameter table from Step 1 and the ten rationale lines from [Module 3](m3-parameters.qmd).

The packet does the document-assembly work for you, the fourth of the four differences [Module 1](m1-how-qcraft-thinks.qmd) sets out. Assumptions, your written remarks and presentation-ready output come out of the same run, so the time that would have gone on copying numbers goes on the Step 7 paragraph instead.

### Step 7: write the two paragraphs

::: {.callout-important}
## DRAFT FOR TEAL: model two-paragraph write-up

Built from the published Uganda figures so every number in it is checkable. Learners replace them with their own run.

> Climate change presents a measurable long-term risk to Uganda's fiscal position. Using the IMF's Quantitative Climate Risk Assessment Fiscal Tool, the baseline projection, which assumes no climate damage, has public debt at 47.5 percent of GDP in 2099 after falling to around 36 percent by mid-century as the demographic dividend widens the gap between growth and the effective interest rate. Under the Hot scenario, in which emissions follow SSP3-7.0 and temperatures track the 90th percentile of model projections, output is around 4 percent below baseline by the end of the century and public debt reaches 66 percent of GDP. The mechanism is indirect: higher temperatures slow labour productivity growth, slower growth reduces revenue, and with primary expenditure held at its baseline level in shilling terms the shortfall accumulates as debt. An annual primary deficit only 0.7 percentage points wider than baseline compounds into a debt ratio more than 18 percentage points higher over seventy years.
>
> The policy significance lies in the threshold rather than the magnitude. In the High, Hot and Vulnerable scenarios, public debt passes the 50 percent of GDP fiscal rule ceiling and takes on a rising trajectory, which means climate damage alone is sufficient to move Uganda from compliance to breach without any other adverse shock. These estimates are conservative. They capture the slow productivity effects of temperature change and exclude natural disasters, sea-level rise, non-market damages and the public expenditure required to adapt, so the true fiscal exposure is larger than reported here. The results are also sensitive to the expenditure rigidity assumption: at full rigidity, the tool's default, the entire revenue loss becomes borrowing, while at 0.6 the end-century gap narrows materially. Meeting Uganda's Paris commitments and building expenditure flexibility both reduce this exposure, and the two are complements rather than alternatives.

**Six things make this a Fiscal Risk Statement paragraph rather than a report of a model run:**

1. It names the tool and the scenario in one clause each, then moves on.
2. Every number is a comparison between two runs, never a forecast.
3. It gives the mechanism in one sentence, so a reader who does not know the debt dynamics equation can still follow the causal chain.
4. It states the threshold, because a breach of an existing commitment is what makes a projection actionable.
5. It states the conservatism caveat before anyone else can, which makes the rest credible.
6. It ends on something the ministry can do.

**One editorial query for Teal:** the closing sentence of the second paragraph does policy advocacy inside a risk document. Whether that register is right is a call I should not make on your behalf.
:::

### Now do your own country

**The seven steps are the part that transfers.** Uganda supplied numbers to check each step against. Nothing in the sequence depended on the country: set the parameters and write down why, check the baseline before you interpret anything, read the three tabs in order, export the packet, write two paragraphs.

The rest of this chapter runs that method twice more, on countries that behave differently from Uganda and from each other, with less help each time. The capstone in [Module 6](m6-capstone.qmd) runs it on yours.

## Completion problem: Ethiopia under the High scenario {#sec-m4-completion}

**You run a new country with the same method, and most of the setup is fixed for you.** Ethiopia earns its place because its demography runs the other way from most countries in a fiscal risk conversation: the working-age population is still climbing, pushing the baseline one way while climate damage pushes the other.

Done for you:

- The method: the same seven steps, in the same order. You are not inventing a procedure.
- The scenario: **High** is SSP3-7.0 at the average of model temperature projections, rather than the 90th percentile.
- The parameter template from Step 1, with one open cell. The debt target is Ethiopia's own fiscal anchor if you can establish one, and 50 percent of GDP if you cannot. Record which you used and why.

Your turn, six tasks:

1. Run the Baseline Sanity Check on Ethiopia. The baseline is different, so all five boxes are now yours to answer, and they come before any climate reading.
2. Read the 2099 debt ratio under High from the Analysis tab. Record it. ____
3. Compute the gap to baseline. ____ percentage points.
4. Read the year the High path crosses your target, if it does. ____
5. Write one sentence explaining why High sits below Hot when both use the same emissions pathway.
6. Rewrite the first sentence of the model paragraph above using your Ethiopia numbers.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## DRAFT FOR TEAL: checking yourself on task 5

The distinction is the temperature distribution, not the emissions. High takes the average temperature outcome across climate models running SSP3-7.0, Hot the 90th percentile of the same set. Same policy world, different draw from the uncertainty. Which belongs in a fiscal risk statement is a real question: risk documents conventionally report adverse tail outcomes, arguing for Hot, while a central-case fiscal framework argues for High. Report both and say why you led with the one you led with.
:::

## Independent problem: adaptation speed, on a third country {#sec-m4-independent}

**This time you get a checklist only, and a country whose fiscal position looks like neither of the first two.** Pick a country from the dropdown whose interest rate exceeds its growth rate, and compare Hot + Adapted against Hot + Unadapted for it. Temperatures are the same in both. The difference is how quickly the economy adjusts.

Deliver five things:

- [ ] The 2099 debt ratio under each, and the gap between them
- [ ] One sentence on what that gap represents in policy terms
- [ ] One sentence on what it does **not** represent, which is the trap in this comparison
- [ ] The same comparison at expenditure rigidity 0.6, with a note on whether the adaptation gap or the rigidity gap is larger for your country
- [ ] A two-paragraph write-up in the format of Step 7

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## DRAFT FOR TEAL: the trap, if you want to check before you write

Faster adaptation in Q-CRAFT is a faster economic adjustment to a given temperature path. It is not adaptation spending. The model does not cost the investment that would produce that adjustment, and the User Guide says so directly [(p. 6)](references.qmd#src-user-guide). So the Adapted-to-Unadapted gap is the benefit side of an adaptation programme with the cost side missing. Reporting it as the value of adaptation without that sentence attached is the likeliest way to misuse this tool in a budget discussion.
:::

## What you can now do

- You have run three countries, one with full support, one where you finished the interpretation, and one alone, and produced an export packet with rationale attached: inputs, rationale, output.
- You can run the Baseline Sanity Check on a country of your own, before interpreting any climate result, and name what each of the five boxes protects you from.
- You can read the three chart families and say what each one licenses you to claim.
- You can write two paragraphs in the register of a published Fiscal Risk Statement, and hand them to the person who owns your ministry's chapter.

Common errors on this material: interpreting climate results before checking the baseline, quoting a 2099 level as a forecast, and reporting the adaptation gap as the value of adaptation.

On your desk this week: take the two paragraphs you drafted to whoever owns your ministry's fiscal risk chapter and ask what they would cut.
